title: Balancing Redox Equations in Acidic Solutions

children.text: The oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions we have encountered thus far are relatively simple and can be balanced simply by using conservation of mass (atom counting by type), making sure the same number of electrons are gained as are lost. However, many redox reactions are more complex and cannot be balanced in this way. We use the
half-reaction method

A technique used to balance oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions by separating the overall reaction into oxidation and reduction half-reactions, balancing each separately, then combining the half-reactions to form the balanced overall redox reaction equation.

for balancing redox reactions because it streamlines balancing of more complicated reactions and because many aspects of electrochemistry are easier to discuss in terms of half-reactions. The half-reaction method splits redox reactions into their oxidation “half” and reduction “half” to make finding the overall equation easier.

Electrochemical reactions frequently occur in solutions, which could be acidic, basic, or neutral. When balancing redox reactions, the nature of the solution may be important. We first look at how to balance a redox reaction in acidic, aqueous solution.
Separate the reaction into an oxidation half-reaction and a reduction half-reaction.
Balance each half-reaction.
Make the numbers of electrons gained and lost equal by multiplying the half-reactions by the appropriate factors.
Add the balanced half-reactions together.
Cancel like terms and simplify.
Check the overall reaction to make sure the mass and charge are balanced.
Steps for Balancing Redox Reactions in Acidic, Aqueous Solution
Balancing a Redox Reaction in Acidic Solution (1)
Balance the following redox reaction in acidic, aqueous solution:
Separate the reaction into oxidation and reduction half-reactions.
Each half-reaction contains the same element in two different oxidation states. Fe
loses an electron to become Fe
, so iron undergoes oxidation. The reduction is not as obvious; however, the oxidation state of manganese decreases from Mn
(in MnO
) to Mn
, so manganese undergoes reduction. The unbalanced half-reactions are:
Balance each half reaction.
Balance elements other than O and H.
Balance O with H
O.
Balance H with H
Balance charge by adding electrons.

The iron atoms in the oxidation half-reaction are balanced (mass balance); however, the charge is unbalanced, since the charges on the ions are not equal. Adding a single electron on the right side gives the balanced oxidation half-reaction:
In the reduction half-reaction, Mn is balanced but the other elements are not. We first add four H
O to the right side of the equation to balance the oxygen atoms, then add 8 H
ions to the left side to balance the hydrogen:

The atoms are now balanced (mass balance), so we now use electrons to balance charge. Since the oxidation number for Mn changes from +7 to +2, we must add five electrons to the left side to balance charge [+7 + −5 = +2].

An alternative way to determine the number of electrons is by comparing the total charges on both sides of the equation. On the left of the reaction arrow the total charge is [(−1) × (1) + (8) × (+1) = +7], and the total charge on the right side is [(1) × (+2) + (4) × (0) = +2]. The difference between +7 and +2 is 5; therefore, we must add five electrons to the left side to achieve charge balance.
We now have two balanced half-reactions:
Make the numbers of electrons gained and lost equal by multiplying the half-reactions by the appropriate factors.

The number of electrons transferred from the oxidation half-reaction to the reduction half-reaction must be equal. In this example, we must multiply every term in the oxidation half-reaction by five. This makes the number of electrons lost equal to the number of electrons gained while maintaining mass balance:
Add the balanced half-reactions together.

The electrons do not appear in the overall redox reaction equation because the oxidation electrons are the same as the reduction electrons, so they “cancel.” The five electrons are not "lost" by five Fe
and "gained" by MnO
but instead are transferred from Fe
to MnO
Check the overall reaction to make sure the mass and charge are balanced

The oxidation number for Mn decreases from +7 in MnO

children.text: Balance charge by adding electrons.
Using change in oxidation number:
The oxidation number for Cr increases from +3 to +6, and there are two Cr atoms. The total difference in charge is therefore 2 × (+3) = +6, so six electrons must be added to the right side.
Using charge balance:
The total charge of the left side is [2 × (+3) = +6], and the total charge of the right side is [−2 + 14 × (+1) = +12]. The difference is +6, so six electrons must be added to the right side:

children.text: Add the balanced half-reactions together.
Note: When the half-reactions are added, (a) all 30 electrons cancel; (b) the 24 H
O molecules on the right in the reduction half-reaction cancel 24 of the 35 H
O molecules on the left in the oxidation half-reaction, leaving 11 H
O molecules on the left; and (c) the 48 H
ions on the left in the reduction half-reaction cancel 48 of the 70 H
ions on the right in the oxidation half-reaction, leaving 22 H
ions on the right.
